source: Keane, Ledgeway, Duff (1994; TCD tech report 1993 version) Constraints on analogical mapping: a comparison of three models
finding: Frames three models (SME, ACME, IAM) by informational constraints (structure, similarity, pragmatics) and behavioural constraints (working-memory limits, background knowledge). Only IAM has the behavioural ones. IAM maps one seed group first, builds one interpretation serially, and backtracks if it fails.
numbers: IAM builds a mapping from a subset of the base: the group of predicates with the most higher-order connectivity. Matches are found by serial constraint satisfaction. SME returns all 32 mappings for the attribute-mapping problem.
quote: IAM forms a mapping from a sub-set of the predicates/elements in a base domain rather than all the elements in the base.
limits: Read from the PostScript technical report (text strings extracted), a substantially revised preprint of the journal paper, not the journal text. Models are run by the authors.
agent_relevance: Maps to a scaffold step that picks one core relational chunk first and maps outward, instead of mapping everything in parallel.

source: Keane, Ledgeway, Duff (1994; TCD tech report 1993 version) Constraints on analogical mapping: a comparison of three models
finding: Experiment 1A (computational): similarity between domains cuts the number of alternative mappings ACME and IAM must produce.
numbers: ACME mappings: None-Similar 8, One-Similar 4, All-Similar 3 (SD 0). IAM mean alternative mappings: 3.2 (SD 2.25), 2.4 (SD 1.43), 1.3 (SD .48), F(2,18)=6.88, p<.01. SME: 32 in every condition.
limits: Model simulations on 10 generated problems per condition.
agent_relevance: Similar surface attributes make mapping easier; an agent facing cross-mapped (similar-but-misaligned) items loses this help.

source: Keane, Ledgeway, Duff (1994; TCD tech report 1993 version) Constraints on analogical mapping: a comparison of three models
finding: Experiment 1B (people): more similar attributes make a hard mapping problem faster to solve. Prediction of ACME and IAM confirmed, not SME.
numbers: N=24 undergraduates recruited, 3 dropped, 21 analysed (7 per condition, between subjects). Mean time to correct solution: None-Similar 210.9 s, One-Similar 164.9 s, All-Similar 69.7 s; F(2,12)=12.02, p<.01.
limits: Tiny cells, between subjects, time to solve (not accuracy). No replication found.
agent_relevance: Human evidence is thin; treat serial-mapping claims as hypotheses.

source: Keane, Ledgeway, Duff (1994; TCD tech report 1993 version) Constraints on analogical mapping: a comparison of three models
finding: Experiment 2B (people): order of presentation changes difficulty of mapping, as the serial IAM predicts and the order-blind ACME does not. Putting the singleton items first nearly halves solution time.
numbers: N=23 recruited, 3 dropped, 20 analysed (10 per condition). Singleton-First mean 178.0 s vs Singleton-Last 363.1 s; Mann-Whitney U=7, p<.005 one-tailed.
quote: The slight change in the ordering of the singletons has a marked effect on the ease of analogical mapping.
limits: 10 per cell, one task (attribute mapping from Holyoak and Thagard 1989), one-tailed test, between subjects. The only direct human order-effect test of IAM found. Not independently replicated in anything opened.
agent_relevance: If order of listing the base items changes success in an LLM, that is a serial-mapping signature. Test by shuffling item order in analogy prompts.

source: Keane, Ledgeway, Duff (1994; TCD tech report 1993 version) Constraints on analogical mapping: a comparison of three models
finding: Experiment 2A (computational): IAM predicts the order effect because it picks the first-met group as seed. SME and ACME predict none.
numbers: IAM mean mappings needed: Singleton-First 1 (SD 0), Singleton-Last 2.9 (SD 1.29), t(18)=-4.67, p<.001. SME 32 and ACME 8 in both orders (SD 0).
limits: The order effect comes from a first-encountered tie-break, so it is a property of that heuristic, not proof of a capacity number. No capacity limit (3 to 4) is quantified in IAM.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 answer: the numbers exist but are small and old; IAM has no fixed relation-count cap.

source: Lewis and Mitchell (2024) Evaluating the robustness of analogical reasoning in large language models (arXiv 2411.14215)
finding: Extends the counterfactual tests: GPT models drop sharply on letter-string variants and on digit matrices with a moved blank, while humans hold steady. Story analogies show an answer-order bias in GPT-4 that humans do not show.
numbers: Story order: GPT-4 89% (16/18) when the correct story is first vs 61% (11/18) second; humans 78% vs 78% (564/720 total). Paraphrased stories: GPT-4 86% (31/36) to 72% (26/36), humans 78% to 70%. Digit matrices: GPT rows about .81 on digits and .48 on alternate blank (about .79 on symbols); the human row is about .72, .77, .70. Human letter-string samples 92 to 384 per cell.
quote: unlike humans, the performance of GPT models are susceptible to answer-order effects
limits: GPT-3, 3.5 and 4 only (2023 models). The table text extracted scrambled, so the row assignment for humans vs GPT-3.5 vs GPT-4 on digit matrices is inferred. Only 18 story items.
agent_relevance: Order and blank-position brittleness is a serial-position effect worth testing in our agent: shuffle candidate order and re-score.

source: Camposampiero, Hersche, Wattenhofer, Sebastian, Rahimi (2025) Can large reasoning models do analogical reasoning under perceptual uncertainty?
finding: First test of reasoning models (o3-mini, DeepSeek R1) on Raven-style symbolic analogy. Both do well on the clean set and collapse when the input is longer, wider and noisier. A neuro-symbolic model does not.
numbers: o3-mini task accuracy 86.6% on I-RAVEN to 17.0% on I-RAVEN-X with confounders and smoothed values, despite 3.4x more reasoning tokens. DeepSeek R1 80.6% to 23.2% (22.8% in the later paper). ARLC neuro-symbolic 98.6% to 88.0%. Chance 12.5%.
quote: a sharp decline in OpenAI's o3-mini task accuracy, dropping from 86.6% on the original I-RAVEN to just 17.0%
limits: Symbolic text benchmark; confounders add input length and distraction together, so the two are mixed. Early-2025 reasoning-model versions.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 and 6: extra tokens did not rescue the model. Distractor attributes hurt the newest reasoning models, so keep irrelevant items out of the mapping step.

source: Camposampiero et al. (2025) I-RAVEN-X: benchmarking generalization and robustness of analogical and mathematical reasoning in LLMs and LRMs
finding: Longer reasoning rules and wider value ranges hurt LLMs far more than reasoning models, but confounders hurt reasoning models too.
numbers: Arithmetic accuracy fall: reasoning models 80.5% to 63.0%, LLMs 59.3% to 4.4%. Ten confounders: o3-mini -11.2 task and -15.2 arithmetic points; R1 -5.8 and -12.2. Smoothing alone: R1 loses up to 19.8 task points, o3-mini 5.4. Both at maximum: o3-mini 17.0%, R1 22.8%. o3-mini matched GPT-4 using 1/21 of the prompt engineering.
limits: Symbolic benchmark; 12.5% chance is the 8-way choice. Only two reasoning models.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: reasoning models widen the usable load but do not remove the limit. More operands per relation is the closest thing to a mapping-size test; scaffolds should still bound it.

source: Shi et al. (2023) Large language models can be easily distracted by irrelevant context (GSM-IC)
finding: One irrelevant sentence added to grade-school math problems cuts accuracy sharply. An instruction to ignore it, self-consistency, and exemplars with distractors help.
numbers: code-davinci-002: fewer than 30% of base problems are consistently solved after adding distractors, under every prompting method. Self-consistency over 20 samples adds more than 11 micro points (35.5 for zero-shot chain of thought). For text-davinci-003, role-overlap distractors push macro accuracy to 0 on problems with more than 2 steps.
limits: 2023 models and a math task, not analogy. Per-method table columns extracted out of order, so individual cell values are not quoted.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: the human attribute-match shift under load has an LLM counterpart in distractor sensitivity. Add an 'ignore irrelevant' instruction and test it.

source: Levy, Jacoby, Goldberg (2024) Same task, more tokens: the impact of input length on the reasoning performance of LLMs
finding: With the task held fixed and only padding added, reasoning accuracy falls well below the context limit. It falls even when the padding repeats the relevant text.
numbers: Average accuracy over tested models falls from 0.92 to 0.68 between a 250-token minimal input and 3000 tokens. Minimal-input accuracy 0.84 to 1.00 (GPT-4 about 1.00). 600 samples per point in the main figure.
limits: True/false reasoning over two text spans, 2024 models (GPT-4, Gemini Pro, Mistral). Not an analogy task. Padding type changes the size of the drop.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: length alone hurts, so a scaffold that trims context per step is supported. Compare with a digit load in humans (Waltz).

source: Lee et al. (2025) The curious case of analogies: investigating analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: Layer analysis of proportional and story analogies: relational information sits in mid-upper layers when the model succeeds and is missing when it fails. LLMs also fail to apply it to new entities, unlike humans. Patching hidden states helps partly.
numbers: No accuracy figures recorded; abstract and introduction only.
limits: Only the abstract and introduction were read. Open-weight models. Mechanistic claim, not a behaviour test.
agent_relevance: Role-binding failures may sit at the apply step, so a binding check after mapping may be needed.

source: Feng and Steinhardt (2024) How do language models bind entities in context? (ICLR 2024)
finding: Language models bind entities to attributes with abstract binding ID vectors added to the activations. The mechanism is found in every sufficiently large LLaMA and Pythia model and gets cleaner with scale.
numbers: Accuracy with entity and attribute interventions applied together is above 97% (restores the original answer). Tested mainly with n=2 and n=3 entities. Chance at n=3 is 0.33.
limits: Open-weight models, small n, synthetic binding tasks. No test of a capacity cap at n=4 or more was seen in the text read. Not analogy.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: models already hold an internal binding table. Whether an explicit external table adds accuracy is untested here.

source: McGovern, Lippincott, Craig, Sirin (2026) When models know more than they say: probing analogical reasoning in LLMs
finding: For rhetorical analogies, probing hidden states beats prompting in open models. For narrative analogies both are similarly low.
numbers: No figures read beyond the abstract.
limits: Abstract and introduction only. Narrative analogy, open-source models.
agent_relevance: Prompted mapping may under-use what the model represents; supports an explicit mapping step, not proof.

source: Chen et al. (2026) ARCANA: a benchmark for abstraction and analogical reasoning (arXiv 2610.29271)
finding: Far-analogy grid tasks: late-2025 frontier models stay below humans. Language-only chain of thought beat vision-language input for most models.
numbers: 200 tasks. Humans: 68.96% average (typos counted correct) or 58.35% strict, 1659 answers. Model totals over 12 attempts (+typo/-typo): GPT 5.2 51.20/48.33, Gemini 3 Pro 43.06/29.19, Grok 4.1 Fast 24.88/18.66, Claude Opus 4.5 8.61/7.18. Language chain of thought for GPT 5.2: 40.19/38.28. Best model 10.13 points under humans (strict); bootstrap CI below zero. ConceptSIR solved 9 of 17 tasks that all four models missed.
limits: Models had to output grids directly, no code tool. One author scored answers. Union over attempts for models vs one attempt for humans. Not letter-string.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: current frontier models still lag humans on far analogy without tools. A slippage-and-reflection loop gave gains, in line with iterative scaffolds.

source: Various sources of distraction during analogical reasoning (2022, via Semantic Scholar)
finding: In human four-term analogies, lures semantically related to the C term hurt most. Perceptual, categorical and relational lures also matter. General reasoning explains the most variance in resisting distraction.
agent_relevance: Gap 5 and 6: independent human work after Waltz, but not a replication of it.

source: Breaking the perceptual-conceptual barrier: relational matching and working memory (2019, via Semantic Scholar)
finding: A concurrent working-memory load stopped people from moving from a perceptual cue to the abstract relation in a relational matching task, unless the load was dropped.
limits: Not opened beyond the abstract. Relational matching-to-sample, not mapping of analogies. Partial conceptual support for Waltz, not a replication.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: the load effect on relational responding shows up in another paradigm.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) Large language models as analogical reasoners (ICLR 2024), cost re-check
finding: The paper admits the method uses more output tokens than 0-shot and 0-shot CoT, and fewer input tokens than few-shot CoT. It never reports an equal-token comparison.
numbers: Self-generated exemplar count K=1 gives 76.1 GSM8K and 34.8 MATH; best at K=3 or 5. With self-consistency: GSM8K 77.8 to 85.3, MATH 37.3 to 46.0.
quote: One limitation of our approach is increased inference computation
limits: Self-consistency adds more samples, so that gain is not token-matched either. Needs a strong model.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: unresolved. Run self-generated analog vs plain extra reasoning at the same total tokens.
